subject: Medicine
summary: Mitral regurgitation is a backflow of blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole, often due to valve prolapse, rheumatic disease or papillary muscle rupture. It leads to volume overload, atrial enlargement and eventually heart failure if untreated.

sections.p: Mitral regurgitation (MR) is incomplete closure of the mitral valve during systole, allowing blood to leak from the left ventricle (LV) back into the left atrium (LA). Diagnosis relies on a holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, confirmed by echocardiography.

t.b: Shows regurgitant jet, valve morphology, LV size and function; a jet >50% of LV area suggests severe MR.
Peak velocity >3 m/s indicates severe MR; lower values suggest mild to moderate.
Enlarged cardiac silhouette and pulmonary vascular congestion point to chronic volume overload.

sections.p: Severity is graded by regurgitant fraction and LV dimensions. The American Society of Echocardiography uses mild (≤30%), moderate (31–50%) and severe (>50%).

t.b: Quantifies volume of blood leaking; >50% indicates severe MR.
LV dilation >55 mm suggests chronic overload.

sections.p: The leading causes vary by region: rheumatic fever in low‑resource settings, degenerative mitral valve prolapse in developed areas, and papillary muscle rupture after myocardial infarction. Other contributors include dilated cardiomyopathy, infective endocarditis, and congenital anomalies.

t.b: Identifies structural lesions (e.g., leaflet thickening, flail segment).
Rule out infective endocarditis if fever or embolic signs present.

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or present with exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, palpitations, and a new holosystolic murmur. In severe cases, a gallop rhythm and tender hepatomegaly may appear.

t.b: Detects murmur, gallop, and signs of right‑sided congestion.
Shows atrial enlargement or arrhythmias secondary to LA dilation.

sections.p: Echocardiography is the cornerstone. When unavailable, a focused cardiac auscultation and chest X‑ray can guide urgency. Blood tests rule out infection or systemic disease.

t.b: Answers whether MR is primary or secondary, its severity, and LV function.
Shows cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion, suggesting chronic MR.
Identify infective endocarditis if fever or emboli are present.

sections.p: Urgent red flags include acute pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, new atrial fibrillation, or embolic events. Complications of chronic MR are atrial fibrillation, heart failure, and infective endocarditis.

t.b: Detects sudden dyspnea or hypotension indicating acute decompensation.
New atrial fibrillation suggests LA enlargement.

faq.a: Yes, many patients have mild MR without symptoms until volume overload progresses.

faq.q: What is the role of beta‑blockers in MR?
faq.a: They reduce heart rate, lower myocardial oxygen demand, and improve LV filling time.
Severe MR with symptoms, LV dysfunction, or atrial fibrillation unresponsive to medical therapy.

exam: Explain the pathophysiology of volume overload in MR and its impact on left atrial size.
Describe the echocardiographic criteria for grading MR severity.
Outline the management steps for a patient with severe MR and acute pulmonary edema.
